q: 201. The moment diagram for a cantilever carrying a concentrated load at its free end, will be
explain: The bending moment varies linearly from zero at the free end to (W * L) at the fixed support, resulting in a triangular Bending Moment Diagram (BMD).

q: 202. Shear force for a cantilever carrying a uniformly distributed load over its length, is
explain: The shear force at any section x from the free end is (w * x). This linear relationship (1st degree) forms a right-angled triangle.

q: 203. When a rectangular beam is loaded longitudinally, shear develops on
explain: Longitudinal or complementary shear stress is developed across every horizontal plane of the beam to maintain equilibrium against the varying bending stresses.

q: 204. When a rectangular beam is loaded transversely, the maximum compressive stress develops on
explain: In a standard sagging beam, the fibers above the neutral axis are in compression, with the maximum value occurring at the outermost 'top' fiber.

q: 205. If the shear force along a section of a beam is zero, the bending moment at the section is
explain: The relationship dM/dx = V implies that when V (Shear Force) is zero, the Bending Moment (M) reaches a stationary point, which is typically its maximum value.

q: 206. A beam is supported over three rollers lying in the same plane. The beam is stable for
options: loading with no component In the direction of the beam
loading with no component perpendicular to the direction of beam
only when no load except self weight acts
explain: Rollers cannot resist horizontal movement. Therefore, the beam is only stable if there is no horizontal force component (no load in the direction of the beam axis).

q: 207. A simply supported beam is subjected to a udl of intensity W/m throughout the length of the span. The B.M. diagram will be a
explain: A UDL produces a 2nd-degree curve (parabola) for the bending moment, with the peak value at the center being wl²/8.

q: 208. The bending moment in a beam will be maximum where
explain: The maximum bending moment occurs at the section where the shear force is zero or changes its sign.

q: 209. The slope of curve of S.F. diagram at any section will be equal to
options: the slope of loading at that section
the ordinate of loading diagram at that section
the area of loading diagram from end to that section
the bending moment at that section
explain: The rate of change of shear force (dV/dx) is equal to the intensity of loading (w) at that specific section.

q: 210. The slope of curve of B.M. diagram at any section will be equal to
options: the slope of moment at that section
the slope of S.F. diagram at that section
the ordinate of S.F. diagram at that section
the area of S.F. diagram starting from any one end
explain: The rate of change of bending moment (dM/dx) at a section is equal to the shear force (V) at that section.

q: 211. A simply supported beam is subjected to a uniformly varying load with zero intensity at the two ends increasing to W/m at the centre. the maximum S.F. is
explain: The total load is (1/2 * l * w). Since the loading is symmetrical, each reaction (Max SF) is half the total load: (1/2 * wl/2) = wl/4.

q: 212. A simply supported beam is subjected to a uniformly varying load with zero intensity at the two ends increasing to W/m at the centre. The max. B.M. will occur at
explain: For a symmetrical loading on a simply supported beam, the maximum bending moment always occurs at the mid-span (l/2 from either end).

q: 213. A simply supported beam is subjected to a uniformly varying load with zero intensity at the two ends increasing to W/m at the centre. The maximum B.M. will be equal to
explain: For this specific triangular loading (apex at center), the maximum bending moment at the mid-span is calculated as wl²/12.

q: 214. Which of the following end conditions permits the displacement in any direction and also rotation?
explain: A free end has no constraints; it can move horizontally, vertically, and rotate freely under load.

q: 215. Which of the following beams will have points of contraflexure? (self weight is negligible)
options: a simply supported beam with udl over entire span
a overhanging beam with loading only over supported span and not on overhangs
fixed beam subjected to concentrated load
cantilever subjected to uniformly varying loads
explain: Fixed beams develop hogging moments at the supports and sagging moments in the center, necessitating points of contraflexure where the BM is zero.

q: 216. A beam is said to have been subjected to a pure bending moment, when
options: the load is applied as a udl throughout the span
S.F. in a length is zero
the load is applied at the mid-span section only
explain: Pure bending occurs in a region where the shear force is zero, meaning the bending moment is constant over that length.

q: 217. The slope of the B.M. diagram change its sign when
explain: The slope of BMD is the Shear Force. If SF changes sign (from positive to negative), the slope of the BM curve changes from increasing to decreasing.

q: 218. A bending moment may be defined as
options: arithmetic sum of the moments of all the forces on either side of the section
arithmetic sum of the forces on either sides of the section
algebraic sum of the moments of all the forces on either side of the section
explain: The internal bending moment at a section is the algebraic sum of the moments of all external forces acting on one side of the section.

q: 219. If Z and I are the section modulus and moment of inertia of the section, the shear force F and bending moment M at a section are related by
explain: The fundamental differential relationship between bending moment and shear force is that F (or V) is the derivative of M with respect to distance x.

q: 220. At either end of a plane frame, maximum number of possible transverse shear forces, are
explain: In a 2D plane frame member, there is only one transverse (perpendicular to the axis) shear force component at any section.

q: 221. At either end of a plane frame, maximum number of possible bending moments, are
explain: In a 2D plane frame, bending occurs only in the plane of the frame, resulting in a single bending moment component (Mz).

q: 222. the shape of the bending moment diagram over the length of a beam, having no external load, is always
explain: With no external load between two points, the shear force is constant (horizontal line), making the bending moment linear (inclined line).

q: 223. The shape of the bending moment diagram over the length of a beam, carrying a uniformly distributed load is always
explain: UDL (constant) leads to a linear SFD, which integrates into a 2nd-degree parabolic curve for the BMD.

q: 224. The shape of the bending moment diagram over the length of a beam, carrying a uniformly increasing load, is always
explain: A uniformly increasing load (1st degree) leads to a parabolic SFD (2nd degree) and a cubical parabolic BMD (3rd degree).

q: 225. The maximum bending moment due to a moving load on a simply supported beam, occurs
explain: For a single concentrated moving load, the absolute maximum bending moment at any section always occurs when the load is placed directly over that section.

q: 226. For a simply supported beam with a central load, the bending moment is
explain: For a simply supported beam of length L with a central point load P, the bending moment increases linearly from zero at the supports to a maximum value of PL/4 at the center.

q: 227. For a cantilever with a uniformly distributed load W over its entire length L, the maximum bending moment is
explain: In a cantilever beam with a UDL, the maximum bending moment occurs at the fixed support and is calculated as (Total Load × Distance to CG), which is W × (L/2) = WL/2.

q: 228. The bending moment is maximum on a section where shearing force
explain: According to the relationship dM/dx = V, the bending moment (M) reaches a local maximum or minimum value where the shear force (V) is zero or changes its sign.

q: 229. A beam is said to be of uniform strength, if
options: B.M. is same throughout the beam
shear stress is same throughout the beam
deflection is same throughout the beam
bending stress is same at every section along its longitudinal axis
explain: A beam of uniform strength is designed by varying its cross-section such that the maximum fiber stress (bending stress) remains constant at every section along its length.

q: 230. In a continuous bending moment curve the point where it changes sign, is called
explain: The point where the bending moment changes from sagging (+) to hogging (-) or vice versa is known by all these terms; it is the location where the curvature of the beam changes.

q: 231. For a beam, if fundamental equations of statics are not sufficient to determine all the reactive forces at the supports, the structure is said to be
explain: Statically indeterminate structures have more unknown support reactions or internal forces than the available equations of equilibrium (ΣH=0, ΣV=0, ΣM=0).

q: 232. If the beam is supported so that there are only three unknown reactive elements at the supports. These can be determined by using the following fundamental equation of statics
explain: For a 2D structure, the three independent equations of equilibrium are the summation of horizontal forces, vertical forces, and moments about any point.

q: 233. For a beam having fixed ends, the unknown element of the reactions, is
options: horizontal component at one end and vertical component at the other
horizontal and vertical components at both the ends
explain: A fixed support prevents translation in both directions and rotation, resulting in three unknowns per support (Horizontal, Vertical, and Moment).

q: 234. A long vertical member, subjected to an axial compressive load, is called
explain: While struts and stanchions are also compressive members, a 'column' specifically refers to a vertical structural member whose primary function is to support axial compressive loads.

q: 235. The ratio of the effective length of a column and minimum radius of gyration of its cross-sectional area, is known
explain: Slenderness ratio (λ = Le/r) is a dimensionless measure used to determine the buckling tendency of a column.

q: 236. The region of the cross-section of a column in which compressive load may be applied without producing any tensile stress, is known as the core... in circular columns the radius of the core, is
explain: To avoid tension in a circular section (Middle Fourth Rule), the eccentricity must not exceed D/8 from the center, making the radius of the core R/4 (or D/8).

q: 237. In rectangular columns (cross-section b x h), the core is a
options: rectangle of lengths b/2 and h/2
rhombus of diagonals b/3 and h/3
explain: For a rectangular section, the Middle Third Rule applies. The 'kern' or core is a rhombus with diagonals equal to b/3 and h/3.

q: 238. A column is said to be of medium size if its slenderness ratio is between
explain: Columns are generally classified as short (λ < 32), medium/intermediate (32 < λ < 120), and long (λ > 120).

q: 239. Euler's formula states that the buckling load P for a column of length l, both ends hinged... is given by the relation
explain: Euler’s critical load formula for a column hinged at both ends uses the full length l as the effective length, resulting in P = π²EI/l².

q: 240. Columns of given length, cross-section and material have different values of buckling loads... the strongest column is one whose
options: one end is fixed and other end is hinged
both ends are hinged or pin jointed
one end is fixed and the other end entirely free
explain: A column with both ends fixed has the shortest effective length (0.5L), which results in the highest buckling load capacity compared to other end conditions.

q: 241. Rankine-Gordon formula accounts for direct as well as buckling stress and is applicable to
explain: Rankine's formula is an empirical formula that works for the entire range of columns but is specifically valuable for intermediate columns where both crushing and buckling occur.

q: 242. The equivalent length of a column fixed at both ends, is
explain: When both ends are fixed, the points of contraflexure occur at 0.25L from each end, making the effective length equal to 0.5L.

q: 243. The equivalent length of a column fixed at one end and free at the other end, is
explain: For a cantilever-type column (one end fixed, one free), the member behaves like half of a hinged-hinged column of double the length, so Le = 2L.

q: 244. The slenderness ratio of a vertical column of a square cross-section of 2.5 cm sides and 300 cm length, is
explain: Radius of gyration r = a/√12 = 2.5/3.464 = 0.721. Slenderness ratio = L/r = 300/0.721 ≈ 416.

q: 245. The slenderness ratio of a vertical column of square cross-section of 10 cm side and 500 cm long, is
246. For keeping the stress wholly compressive, the load may be applied on a circular column anywhere within a concentric circle of diameter
explain: According to the Middle Fourth Rule for circular sections, the diameter of the core (within which no tension occurs) is d/4.

q: 247. To ascertain the maximum permissible eccentricity of loads on circular columns, the rule generally followed, is
explain: The 'Middle Fourth Rule' specifically applies to circular sections to ensure that the stress remains compressive across the entire section.

q: 248. The greatest eccentricity which a load W can have without producing tension on the cross-section of a short column of external diameter D and internal diameter d, is
explain: For a hollow circular section, the kern radius is (D²+d²)/8D to maintain purely compressive stresses.

q: 249. The effect of arching a beam, is
options: to reduce the bending moment throughout
to increase the bending moment throughout
explain: Arching action converts some of the bending moments into axial thrust, thereby reducing the net bending moment that the material must resist.

q: 250. A three-hinged arch is said to be
explain: With three hinges (two at supports, one at crown), there are 4 unknown reactions and 4 available equations (3 from statics + 1 from the internal hinge moment = 0), making it determinate.

q: 251. In a three hinged arch, the bending moment will be zero
options: at both right and left hinges
explain: By definition, a hinge cannot resist or transfer bending moment; therefore, the BM is zero at every hinge location.

q: 252. In a three hinged arch, the third hinge is generally kept at
options: midpoint of the crown and left support hinge
midpoint of the crown and right support hinge
explain: To maintain symmetry and structural efficiency, the internal hinge is usually placed at the highest point of the arch, known as the crown.

q: 253. If a three hinged parabolic arch carries a uniformly distributed load on its entire span, every section of the arch resists
explain: A parabolic arch under full UDL is in a state of pure compression (the 'funicular shape' for UDL is a parabola), meaning BM and Shear are zero.

q: 254. The rise of a parabolic arch at quarter points, is equal to
options: 1/3 times the rise of the crown
1/4 times the rise of the crown
1/2 times the rise of the crown
3/4 times the rise of the crown
explain: Using the equation y = 4hx(L-x)/L², at x = L/4, y = 4h(L/4)(3L/4)/L² = 3h/4.

q: 255. A linear arch is subjected only to
explain: A linear arch (or theoretical arch) is shaped such that its centerline coincides with the line of thrust, resulting in only axial compression (thrust).

q: 256. An arch with three hinges, is a structure
explain: As established in Q. 250, the three hinges provide enough equations to solve for all reactions using statics alone.

q: 257. In a three hinged arch, the shear force is usually
explain: Shear force in an arch is the component of the resultant force perpendicular to the arch axis; this typically reaches its peak near the support points (springings).

q: 258. In a solid arch, shear force acts
options: along the axis of the arch
perpendicular to the axis of arch
explain: Normal thrust acts tangentially/along the axis, while radial shear acts perpendicular to the axis of the arch.

q: 259. An arch may be subjected to
options: thrust, shear force and bending moment
explain: Unlike a funicular arch, a general arch structure under arbitrary loading must resist axial compression (thrust), transverse shear, and bending moments.

q: 260. For a stable frame structure, number of members required, is
options: three times the number of joints minus three
twice the number of joints minus three
twice the number of joints minus two
twice the number of joints minus one
explain: The condition for a perfect (statically determinate) plane truss is m = 2j - 3, where m is members and j is joints.

q: 261. If two forces acting at a joint are not along the straight line, then for the equilibrium of the joint
options: one of the forces must be zero
forces must be equal and of the same sign
forces must be equal in magnitude but opposite in sign
explain: If only two non-collinear members meet at a joint with no external load, both must carry zero force to satisfy ΣH=0 and ΣV=0.

q: 262. Stress in members of statically determinate simple frames, can be determined by
explain: All three are standard methods for analyzing trusses; Method of Joints uses joint equilibrium, Method of Sections uses part equilibrium, and Graphical (Cremona) uses vector diagrams.

q: 263. A member is balanced at its end by two inclined members carrying equal forces. For equilibrium the angle between the inclined bars must be
explain: For three equal forces to be in equilibrium at a joint, the angle between each pair of forces must be 120° (Lami's Theorem).

q: 264. A principal plane is a plane which carries
options: the given of higher magnitude acting
explain: By definition, principal planes are those on which the shear stress is zero; they only carry normal stresses (principal stresses).

q: 265. The angle between the two principal planes is
explain: The major and minor principal planes are always mutually perpendicular (90 degrees apart).

q: 266. If an element of a specimen of brittle material is subjected to shear stress, the crack propagation if occurs, will be inclined to the sides of the element at
explain: Brittle materials are weak in tension. Pure shear produces maximum principal tensile stress at 45°, leading to failure along that plane.

q: 267. A prismatic bar is supported at top and is subjected to its own weight... the total elongation of the bar is given by
explain: The elongation due to self-weight is WL/2AE. Substituting W = ρAL, we get (ρAL)L/2AE = ρl²/2E.

q: 268. The assumption that the cross-sections plane before bending remain plane even after bending means
options: the strains in the fibers are proportional to their distances from neutral axis
the bending moment will be resisted by the central core of the section
the stresses in the fibres are proportional to their distances from neutral axis
the neutral axis lies at mid height
explain: Bernoulli's assumption implies that longitudinal strain varies linearly with the distance from the neutral axis.

q: 269. The assumption in the theory of bending that the material is homogeneous and isotropic... implies that
options: the stresses are proportional to strains at all fibres
the strains are proportional to distances of the fibres from neutral axis
the beam bends into a circular arc
the neutral axis lies at the centre
explain: Homogeneity and isotropy imply consistent elastic properties throughout, which allows Hooke's Law (Stress ∝ Strain) to be applied uniformly.

q: 270. The moment of inertia of a rectangular section b x d about the base is
explain: Using Parallel Axis Theorem: I_base = I_cg + Ah² = (1/12 bd³) + (bd)(d/2)² = 1/3 bd³.

q: 271. For a circular section Izz = Ixx = Iyy. Then zz-axis
options: will be tangential to the circle
will be passing through point of intersection... and perpendicular to the plane
explain: Izz represents the polar moment of inertia, which is the sum of Ixx and Iyy (Perpendicular Axis Theorem), passing through the centroid perpendicular to the section.

q: 272. The moment of inertia of triangular section b x d, about the base is
explain: Using Parallel Axis Theorem: I_base = I_cg + Ah² = (bh³/36) + (1/2 bh)(h/3)² = bh³/12.

q: 273. In the case of T section, the maximum bending stress will occur at
explain: Since stress σ = My/I, the maximum stress occurs at the fiber furthest from the neutral axis. In a T-section, the NA is closer to the flange, making the web's bottom fiber the furthest.

q: 274. The neutral axis of any section is
options: the axis passing through middle point of the height
the line of intersection of neutral plane with cross-section
the axis about which the moment of inertia is minimum
explain: The neutral axis is the geometric line where the neutral surface (which undergoes no longitudinal strain) intersects the cross-sectional plane.

q: 275. Which of the following sections is the most efficient in carrying bending moments?
explain: An I-section is most efficient because most of its area is located far from the neutral axis (in the flanges), providing a large section modulus with less material.

q: 276. The bending moment at a section tends to bend or deflect the beam and the internal stress resist its bending. The resistance offered by the internal stresses, to the bending, is called
explain: Bending stress (or flexural stress) is the internal resistance developed by the fibers of a beam to counteract the external bending moment.

q: 277. In a simple bending theory, one of the assumptions is that the material of the beam is isotropic. This assumption means that the
options: normal stress remains constant in all directions
normal stress varies linearly in the material
elastic constants are same in all the directions
elastic constants varies linearly in the material
explain: An isotropic material has identical physical and elastic properties (like Young's Modulus and Poisson's ratio) in all directions at any given point.

q: 278. In a simple bending of beams, the stress in the beam varies
explain: According to the flexure formula (σ = My/I), the bending stress is directly proportional to the distance from the neutral axis, resulting in a linear distribution.

q: 279. When a beam is subjected to a bending moment, the strain in a layer is ............ the distance from the neutral axis.
explain: The fundamental assumption that 'plane sections remain plane' implies that longitudinal strain (ε) varies linearly with the distance (y) from the neutral axis.

q: 280. The bending equation is
explain: The Bernoulli-Euler bending equation relates the internal moment (M), moment of inertia (I), stress (σ), distance from neutral axis (y), modulus (E), and radius of curvature (R).

q: 281. A section of beam is said to be in pure bending, if it is subjected to
options: constant bending moment and constant shear force
constant shear force and zero bending moment
constant bending moment and zero shear force
explain: Pure bending (or simple bending) occurs in a region where the bending moment is constant, which mathematically implies the shear force (dM/dx) must be zero.

q: 282. When a beam is subjected to bending moment, the stress at any point is ............ the distance of the point from the neutral axis.
explain: As per the flexure formula σ = (M/I)y, for a given section, stress increases linearly as you move further away from the neutral axis.

q: 283. The neutral axis of the cross-section of a beam is that axis at which the bending stress is
explain: The neutral axis is the layer in the beam that undergoes no extension or contraction; therefore, the strain and the corresponding stress are zero.

q: 284. The section modulus (Z) of a beam is given by
explain: Section modulus (Z) is defined as the ratio of the moment of inertia (I) to the distance of the extreme fiber from the neutral axis (y_max).

q: 285. The section modulus of a rectangular section about an axis through its C.G., is
explain: For a rectangle, I = bd³/12 and y_max = d/2. Thus, Z = (bd³/12) / (d/2) = bd²/6.

q: 286. If the section modulus of a beam is increased, the bending stress in the beam will
explain: Since σ = M/Z, bending stress is inversely proportional to the section modulus. A higher Z indicates a stronger section with lower stress for the same moment.

q: 287. Two beams, one of circular cross-section and the other of square cross-section, have equal areas of cross-sections. When these beams are subjected to bending
explain: For the same cross-sectional area, a square section has a higher section modulus than a circular section, making it more efficient (economical) in resisting bending.

q: 288. When a cantilever beam is loaded at its free end, the maximum compressive stress shall develop at
explain: In a cantilever beam loaded downwards, the top fibers undergo tension (stretching) and the bottom fibers undergo compression (shortening).

q: 289. A beam of uniform strength may be obtained by
options: keeping the width uniform and varying the depth
keeping the depth uniform and varying the width
varying the width and depth both
explain: Uniform strength is achieved by adjusting the section modulus (Z) along the length to match the bending moment (M) so that the stress σ = M/Z remains constant.

q: 290. If the depth is kept constant for a beam of uniform strength, then its width will vary in proportional to
explain: σ = M / (bd²/6). If σ and d are constant, then b must be directly proportional to M (b ∝ M).

q: 291. A beam of uniform strength has
options: same bending stress at every section
same bending moment at every section
same shear stress at every section
explain: The core definition of a beam of uniform strength is that the maximum fiber stress is constant across every cross-section along its longitudinal axis.

q: 292. The bending stress in a beam is ............ bending moment.
explain: From the equation σ = My/I, it is clear that for a given section, the stress is directly proportional to the applied bending moment.

q: 293. At the neutral axis of a beam
options: the layers are subjected to maximum bending stress
the layers are subjected to minimum bending stress
the layers are subjected to compression
the layers do not undergo any strain
explain: The neutral axis is the 'zero-strain' axis. Fibers at this location neither elongate nor contract when the beam is bent.

q: 294. The neutral axis of a beam is subjected to ............ stress.
explain: Since there is zero strain at the neutral axis, and stress = Modulus × Strain, the bending stress at the neutral axis is also zero.

q: 295. The neutral axis of a transverse section of a beam passes through the centre of gravity of the section and is
options: in the same plane in which the beam bends
at right angle to the plane in which the beam bends
explain: If a beam bends in a vertical plane, the neutral axis is a horizontal line perpendicular to that plane of bending.

q: 296. When a rectangular beam is loaded transversely, the maximum tensile stress is developed on the
explain: For a simply supported beam under downward loads, the beam sags. This creates compression in the top fibers and tension in the bottom fibers.

q: 297. When a rectangular beam is loaded transversely, the maximum compressive stress is developed on the
explain: As explained in Q. 296, the curvature causes the top layer of a simply supported beam to shorten, resulting in maximum compressive stress.

q: 298. The maximum shear stress will always occur at
options: a fibre in the cross-section depending on the configuration
explain: While max shear is at the neutral axis for common shapes like rectangles/circles, for certain complex sections (like some I-beams), it can occur elsewhere depending on the geometry.

q: 299. The shear stress at any section of a shaft is maximum
options: at the centre of the section
at a distance r/2 from the centre
at the top of the surface
at a distance 3/4r from the centre
explain: In torsion, shear stress τ = (T·r)/J. It is zero at the center (axis of rotation) and increases linearly to a maximum at the outer surface (radius R).

q: 300. At the neutral axis of a beam, the shear stress is
explain: For standard sections like rectangles and circles, the shear stress distribution is parabolic, reaching its maximum value at the neutral axis.
